extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent litigators, damages experts, and juries
extracted.subtask_description: Model and recommended jury instructions and evaluative criteria for determining reasonable royalty patent damages, focusing on selecting the pre-investment negotiation date, apportioning value, and practical guidance for jurors and courts. Targets jury instructions, damages methodologies, and comparability of licenses (including SEP-specific timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of reasonable royalty (pre-investment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the payment that the patent holder and the accused infringer would have agreed to immediately before the accused infringer invested in using the allegedly infringing technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instruction focuses jurors on the patent's ex ante market value immediately prior to the defendant's investment decision; this framing is preferred because it excludes lock-in costs and ex post contamination that overcompensate the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set the negotiation/valuation date immediately before investment (pre-investment negotiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is to determine the appropriate date for the parties' pre-investment negotiation: the negotiation date should be a date on which the accused infringer is deciding between using the patented technology versus any alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting the date immediately before the decision to use the technology is preferable to the date of first infringement because it excludes lock-in costs. For SEP cases, value the patent just before the technology was incorporated into the standard (the 'pre-standard negotiation') because later implementer decisions do not reflect genuine alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions for hypothetical negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury should assume that both parties believed the patent was valid and would be infringed, that both were willing to enter an agreement, and that both would have acted reasonably in negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury must choose a royalty that would have resulted from the negotiation, not simply a royalty either party would have preferred. Where a patentee would not willingly license ex ante (e.g., competitors or pharmaceutical single-patent products), commercial considerations must inform relative bargaining power and the resulting royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor One — Incremental value contributed by the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages must be based only on the incremental value that the claimed invention contributes to the accused product, determined by comparing the allegedly infringing technology to the accused infringer's best ex ante alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries should consider commercially acceptable non-infringing alternatives available at the negotiation date. The best alternative is determined by both cost to and value for the infringer; the maximum the infringer would pay equals the cost of the best alternative plus the incremental value of the invention over that alternative. Disregard 'switching costs' (e.g., redesign, retooling, inventory) when determining incremental value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives impose a ceiling on the royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives to the patented technology and advantages provided by the patented technology relative to the alternatives should be considered so that alternatives put a ceiling on what a willing licensee would pay ex ante.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should be instructed that a licensee would not pay more than the value of the patent relative to available alternatives; availability of alternatives is a fundamental constraint on reasonable royalty and should not be treated as merely one factor among many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Two — Exclude value contributed by non-patented factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonable royalty may not be based on value added to the accused product by any factor other than the claimed invention (e.g., manufacturing process, product marketing, brand recognition, or other components/technologies not in the claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries must apportion to isolate the patented invention's contribution and exclude unrelated features. If the patented invention allows a simpler manufacturing process, that benefit may be attributable to the invention; otherwise, exclude manufacturing/marketing/brand value from the royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the smallest saleable patent-practicing unit (SSPPU) as the anchor, with apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claimed invention covers one feature in a multi-component product, damages generally must be based at most on the 'smallest saleable patent-practicing unit' that substantially embodies the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when using the SSPPU as the anchor, the jury must apportion out the value of features or technologies within that unit that are unrelated to the claimed invention—the SSPPU identifies the proper anchor but does not obviate the need to isolate the patented feature's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Three — Consideration of comparable license agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury should consider prior agreements by the patent holder to license the patents-in-suit or other agreements if they were negotiated in circumstances and concerned subjects sufficiently comparable to the parties' hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual licenses around the time the accused infringer first elected to use the technology can be highly probative because they reflect marketplace value at the relevant time. But jurors must be instructed how to determine 'comparable' and to account for ex post factors (e.g., lock-in) that may have inflated license prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Four — Economic relationship of the parties and commercial considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury should consider the economic relationship of the parties (e.g., whether the patentee would generally prefer exclusive use or to license broadly) and other commercial evidence that sheds light on bargaining positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial considerations—such as whether the parties are competitors or whether the patentee had a policy not to license—are relevant to relative bargaining power and the appropriate royalty and should not be ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions should be simple, tailored, and provide practical calculation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury instructions should use simple, case-tailored language and give practical guidance on how to calculate a reasonable royalty and how to assess disputed facts and proposed methodologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than reciting lengthy factor lists verbatim, instructions should present cohesive principles (e.g., the streamlined four-factor approach), explain apportionment and comparability, and direct jurors to focus on restoring the parties to the pre-investment bargaining position for an accurate, reviewable award.
